$comment: The MQTT *payload* contract, as data (#317).
Sibling to topics.json, which did this for topic strings in #171 and
stops there. The message bodies on those topics are hand-written three
times - TypeScript across packages/protocol and packages/relay-core,
Swift in adapter-mac's Payloads.swift, Kotlin in adapter-android's
Payloads.kt - and until this file, each asserted only against its own
literals. Three separate source files say so in their own comments:
Payloads.swift ('three hand-written implementations of one wire
format, and nothing else catches them drifting'), CommandTimeout.swift
and BluetoothConnectionManager.kt (both about one number).
A drift here is invisible in CI and shows up on hardware as a node
that registers and is then ignored, or a command that is discarded as
stale - the #174/#175/#182 failure mode, one layer up from topics.
#271 makes Rust the fourth mirror. Every copy added before this file
existed is one more to reconcile afterwards.
This file PINS the shapes that already ship. It is not a change to
the frozen contract (AGENTS.md) and needs no ADR - it asserts, exactly
as topics.json does. If a conformance test disagrees with this file,
the finding is a bug in one implementation, not a licence to edit the
fixture until it passes.
Numbers that MUST be identical in every implementation, because an
aggregate over them is only meaningful if they mean the same thing
in every row (ADR 0019, #206 criterion 2).
commandOutcomeTimeoutMs guarantees TERMINATION, not latency - ADR
0007 owns latency with its own p95 SLO. A claim settles in 3.3-4.9s
on the reference hardware (#254, #310), so 8s is roughly 2x
headroom.
heartbeatTimeoutMs is the relay's side: three missed beats at
heartbeatIntervalMs. It is deliberately a multiple, not an
independent number - see relay-service.ts.
Closed sets, in wire spelling. Order matters for eventKinds only.
eventKinds is PRIORITY ORDER, highest first - architecture.md's
'Priority rules'. packages/protocol exports it as PRIORITY_ORDER and
relay-core must import rather than re-derive. Rule 5 (last-claimed)
is a tiebreak, not an event kind, so it is not in this list.
failureReasons: only target_device_unreachable and
superseded_by_newer_command are emitted today. bluetooth_unavailable
is defined and deliberately unused until the platform gateways can
surface comparable typed errors - see either Payloads file's kdoc.
The wire set is still all three, so a relay must accept all three.
The `kind` discriminators that let several message shapes share the
frozen events topic (ADR 0001/0015 freeze the topic SET, so a new
message kind rides an existing topic rather than getting its own -
docs/handoffs/67.md).
An ordinary event has NO `kind` at all, and its `type` is always an
eventKind, never one of these. That is what makes the discriminator
backward-compatible: adding a kind cannot change how an existing
event parses.
Which way each message travels, because it decides what an
implementation must prove about it.
An implementation must ENCODE the messages it sends to exactly the
object below (compared as parsed JSON - key order is not part of the
contract), and must DECODE the messages it receives without loss.
Encoding is the stronger assertion, so each side gets it for its own
half rather than both sides being held to both.
This distinction is load-bearing, not bookkeeping. `stateNoHolder`
is `{"holder": null}`, and Swift's synthesised encoder OMITS a nil
Optional - so an adapter re-encoding it would produce `{}` and fail
a naive round-trip. That is not a defect: adapters never publish
state, only read it. Holding them to an encode they never perform
would have produced a false failure and, worse, an 'explicit null'
workaround in an adapter that has no reason to serialise this type
at all.
Canonical wire objects, keyed by name. See `directions` above for
what each implementation must prove about which ones.
Every value here is the complete object as it appears on the wire,
except for the `$comment` key, which is documentation for the reader
and must be stripped before any comparison.

event.$comment: Node -> relay on the events topic. No `kind`.

eventEnd.$comment: 'the trigger I reported earlier stopped' (#68). No priority - ending a trigger needs only its kind.

$comment: Node -> relay, re-sent periodically and not only at startup, which
is what lets a restarted relay recover a correct picture (#178).
observedRoutes (#191) is keyed by resource type, and ABSENCE is
meaningful: a missing key means 'cannot determine', which leaves
the relay's record alone. `false` positively asserts this node
does not hold the resource and is grounds for corrective action.
Reporting a guess as `false` hands the relay a fabricated
disagreement - see registrationNoRouteKnown below.
The absent-route case, pinned as its own message because it is a
distinct assertion and the one most easily 'simplified' into a
`false`. An empty observedRoutes is what a node sends while a
claim or release is still settling.
Also the first-registration shape: activeEvents is empty, not
omitted. #303's signature was a node reporting {} repeatedly.

command.$comment: Relay -> node, stamped with ADR 0018's epoch and sequence number (#210).

$comment: A command carrying NEITHER epoch nor seq, which both adapters must
still decode and act on.
Not defensive padding: the relay half of #210 shipped before the
adapter half, so builds exist that ran against a relay stamping
nothing. CommandSequenceGate treats an unsequenced command as
acceptable rather than stale. Making these required would brick
those builds, and an outcome for such a command must stay
reportable - see commandOutcomeUnsequenced.

state.$comment: Relay -> everyone, RETAINED on the state topic (#229). The authoritative answer to 'who holds this resource'.

$comment: `holder: null` is a REAL answer - the relay genuinely publishes it
when nobody holds the resource - and must stay distinct from 'we
have never heard from the relay'. Both platforms keep that
distinction in a HolderState type, because storing both as a nil
String makes the UI state confidently that nobody holds the
headset when the truth is it has no idea (#308's family of bug).

commandOutcomeSucceeded.$comment: ADR 0019. Reported for EVERY command, not only failures - a success rate needs its denominator.

commandOutcomeFailed.$comment: `reason` is present when and only when outcome is `failed`. Headset in its case is unreachable, not a timeout (#264).

$comment: ADR 0020's coalescing, reported as a failure reason but tracked
separately from real failures: a superseded command is the
debouncer working correctly, not a switch that went wrong (#206
criterion 5). Counting it against the success rate would make the
rate drop every time coalescing did its job.
The constants.commandOutcomeTimeoutMs bound, reached. `reason` is
absent: timed_out is its own outcome, not a failure with a reason.
#303 is the case where this was never published at all - a bound
that could not fire left a claim wedged for seventeen minutes with
no outcome on the wire. A missing outcome is not a passing switch.

commandOutcomeUnsequenced.$comment: The outcome for commandUnsequenced. Must stay reportable, or acting on an unsequenced command becomes an unmeasurable switch - the exact gap ADR 0019 exists to close.
